sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
# Description

Implement an arbitrary-precision `Decimal` class.

Floating point numbers are the most common representation of non-integer real numbers in computing, and they're a common standard defined by [IEEE 754](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754). They're very flexible and versatile, but they do have some limitations. Famously, in floating point arithmetic, [`0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`](http://0.30000000000000004.com/).

The solution to this issue is to find another, lossless way to model arbitrary-precision non-integer reals. This may be less efficient in terms of memory or processing speed than floating point numbers; the goal is to provide exact results.

Despite `Decimal` being a custom type, we should still be able to treat them as numbers: the `==`, `<`, `>`, `+`, `-`, and `*` operators should all work as expected on Decimals. For expediency, you are not required to implement division, as arbitrary-precision division can very quickly get out of hand. (How do you represent arbitrary-precision `1/3`?)

In Rust, the way to get these operations on custom types is to implement the relevant traits for your custom object. In particular, you'll need to implement at least `PartialEq`, `PartialOrd`, `Add`, `Sub`, and `Mul`. Strictly speaking, given that the decimal numbers form a total ordering, you should also implement `Eq` and `Ord`, though those traits are not checked for by these tests.

# Note

It would be very easy to implement this exercise by using the [bigdecimal](https://crates.io/crates/bigdecimal) crate. Don't do that; implement this yourself.

####

Use the above instructions to modify the supplied files: src/lib.rs Cargo.toml
Don't change the names of existing functions or classes, as they may be referenced from other code like unit tests, etc.
Only use standard libraries, don't suggest installing any packages.
Do not modify the test files. Run the tests with: cargo test --offline -- --include-ignored

Using decimal digits directly makes parsing/comparison easy, and the tests only go up to about 45 digits, but performance isn't an issue. ## Summary

I implemented `Decimal` from scratch in `src/lib.rs` (no external crates, `Cargo.toml` unchanged):

**Representation** — each value is stored as:
- `neg: bool` — sign flag (zero is always stored non-negative, so `-0` and `0` compare equal)
- `mag: Vec<u32>` — magnitude as an integer in little-endian base-10⁹ chunks
- `scale: u32` — number of fractional digits, i.e. value = `mag / 10^scale`

**Core helpers**:
- `parse_mag` — converts the digit string (integer digits ++ fraction digits) into base-10⁹ chunks, with `scale = fraction length`
- `cmp_mag` / `add_mag` / `sub_mag` / `mul_mag` — schoolbook big-integer operations on the chunk representation
- `rescale(m, k)` — multiplies a magnitude by 10ᵏ (shift by `k/9` whole chunks plus a multiply by `10^(k%9)`), used to bring operands to a common scale
- `add_raw` / `make` — signed addition logic handling same-sign (magnitude add) vs. mixed-sign (magnitude subtract with sign selection), with zero normalization

**Traits implemented**: `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Ord`, `PartialOrd` (all via a scale-aware `cmp_val` that rescales to the max scale before comparing), plus `Add`, `Sub` (via `add_raw` with flipped sign), and `Mul` (scale = sum of scales).
